subject: Disabling error handling with compiler argument

messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Disabling error handling with compiler argument
parts:
[splitting discussion, renamed subject]

Hi all, I thought this deserved its own thread.

First off, I'll start with my stance. I don't think turning off all error checking with a single switch is a good thing. It may save time, but I'm not convinced Stan will work properly. The error handling is actually embedded deep within transforms and other things. With that said, I think the proper way to do it is not within the check_* functions themselves, but give the control to the caller. I think it makes sense that we have at least two levels of checking, and maybe more. I haven't thought about it enough.

Ben, by disabling the check_* functions altogether, we lose all the checks in transforms and data IO.

Marcus, thanks for bringing that use case up. Does it ever fail the SPD checks? Or does it get caught somewhere else?

So, I know we do some duplicate validation when we use one distribution and that calls another. That was where I was thinking it'd be nice to have an argument indicate whether it should be validated from the outside.


On May 23, 2014 11:19 AM, "Marcus Brubaker" <marcus.a...@gmail.com> wrote:
Actually, the ability to do this can have really big gains in some models.  For instance, the CAR models that use the matrix_normal_prec distribution.  Being able to turn off the SPD checks means we don't have to actually compute the Cholesky factorization of a fairly large, sparse (and constant) matrix.  In fact there was a user trying to run these models and Stan was intolerably slow so I had at one point made a special branch for him which turned off these checks.

Cheers,
Marcus



On Fri, May 23, 2014 at 8:16 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

On May 23, 2014, at 5:18 AM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:

> ... I'm not sure if anything is so essential that it must be checked unconditionally. We should definitely be willing to segfault if there is a problem with the model and NDEBUG is defined. No throwing exceptions, etc.

As long as we plaster open-wheel racing mode (nitro drag race
mode for you Americans) with sufficient warnings and make clients
sign a waiver (modal dialog box for interactive embedded or
cluster use), I'd be OK with that.

Personally, I don't think I would ever run in such a mode unless
there were huge performance gains (more than a factor of two, say)
and I really trusted the model.

I do think there's utility in building a C++ API mode that fails quietly
without throwing exceptions for embedding.  I think Daniel has that
covered in the design.  We're pretty much only using the exceptions to
propagate to the point where we do a rejection.

- Bob

messages.author: 2a7f346506a3e9ff
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Disabling error handling with compiler argument
parts:
Agreed Daniel, this issue definitely deserves it's own thread.

I agree that template-based checking would be best.  It's a somewhat delicate problem though with a number of use-cases and desired behaviours.

In the case of the CAR models, because of the use of the precision matrix and the fact that one of the matrices is constant (i.e., it's data) we don't actually ever *need* it's Cholesky factor unless someone wants the normalizing constant.  However, to be pedantic, we need to always check that it's SPD and the most efficient way to do that is with the Cholesky factorization.  For cases like this (i.e., data parameters) what we'd really like is behaviour where it's confirmed to satisfy the constraints once and then never again.  (My memory is hazy, but I believe the CAR model is further complicated because the matrix is only positive semi-definite, but lets ignore that for now.)

Non-constant parameters should always be checked at every iteration regardless of compilation flags though because sampling can drive them into bad spaces.  Turning of checks in these cases will result in invalid samples.

On the other hand, bound checks have a non-trivial cost in some models (I've seen them pop up while profiling) and can often times be turned off.  These may be the kind of thing to turn off by a compiler flag for adventurous users.

I suggest that we try to concretely define a few desired use-cases for toggling error checking.  There is more than one and a solution for one may not work for another.  (Of course, on the flip side, solving all of them may be prohibitively complex...)

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Disabling error handling with compiler argument
parts:
On Friday, May 23, 2014 4:32:43 PM UTC-4, Daniel Lee wrote:
First off, I'll start with my stance. I don't think turning off all error checking with a single switch is a good thing. It may save time, but I'm not convinced Stan will work properly. The error handling is actually embedded deep within transforms and other things. With that said, I think the proper way to do it is not within the check_* functions themselves, but give the control to the caller. I think it makes sense that we have at least two levels of checking, and maybe more. I haven't thought about it enough.

Ben, by disabling the check_* functions altogether, we lose all the checks in transforms and data IO.

Yes, that is what I was trying to achieve, even though the checks in data or transformed data would only be executed once. The checks in transformed parameters are called a lot and don't add much value; either you wrote the transformation correctly and it is guaranteed that the transformed parameter is valid or you didn't and you will probably get a NaNs.  Presumably someone would have first done the model with exceptions and checks and validations and only turned them off after they were satisfied that their code is correct. But even if they haven't, I personally don't care. They asked for a non-default behavior of no checks, so they deserve what they get. That said, I'm not too particular about how we go about it or if we offer levels of checking or what.

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: Disabling error handling with compiler argument
parts:
With call-by-call control, maybe the user could
use a no-check argument or we could introduce something
like template parameters. I've already been thinking about
this kind of syntax to start controlling up-to-a-proportion
or not behavior, which should be user controllable.

More inline below.

On May 24, 2014, at 1:49 AM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:

> On Friday, May 23, 2014 4:32:43 PM UTC-4, Daniel Lee wrote:
> First off, I'll start with my stance. I don't think turning off all error checking with a single switch is a good thing. It may save time, but I'm not convinced Stan will work properly. The error handling is actually embedded deep within transforms and other things. With that said, I think the proper way to do it is not within the check_* functions themselves, but give the control to the caller. I think it makes sense that we have at least two levels of checking, and maybe more. I haven't thought about it enough.
>
> Ben, by disabling the check_* functions altogether, we lose all the checks in transforms and data IO.
>
> Yes, that is what I was trying to achieve, even though the checks in data or transformed data would only be executed once. The checks in transformed parameters are called a lot and don't add much value; either you wrote the transformation correctly and it is guaranteed that the transformed parameter is valid or you didn't and you will probably get a NaNs.

There are potentially two checks done on a transformed parameter.

1. The check at the end of the block to make sure it's
defined properly.

2. The check on whatever distribution it's fed into to
make sure the argument's right.

It's that first one that won't get made if you don't include it
in the constraints.
> Presumably someone would have first done the model with exceptions and checks and validations and only turned them off after they were satisfied that their code is correct.

There's a bit of an issue with random behavior. The transformation
may be right, but in some cases (say some initializations), may underflow
or overflow.

But I think when that happens, you'll get a rejection just without any
kind of message, which is really the right behavior.

So I'm not sure this is really a problem.

> But even if they haven't, I personally don't care. They asked for a non-default behavior of no checks, so they deserve what they get. That said, I'm not too particular about how we go about it or if we offer levels of checking or what.

As I said before, I'm OK with daredevil mode for those who want it.

- Bob
